title: Reassure an anxious patient
description: Make space for worry, explain the next step, and check understanding.
facts: Alex is waiting for a routine blood test.
The team has not provided a result or a waiting time.
Your task is communication practice, not clinical advice.

turns.line: I’m really nervous. I don’t like needles. Is this going to hurt?
turns.goal: Acknowledge the worry without promising an outcome.
turns.example: I can hear that you’re worried. We can take this one step at a time. What worries you most?
turns.phrase: I can hear that you’re worried. What concerns you most?

turns.line: I’m worried I might faint. Can you tell me what happens next?
turns.goal: Explain that you will check with the team; avoid inventing clinical details.
turns.example: Thank you for telling me. I’ll let the team know how you’re feeling and check the next step with them.
turns.phrase: Let me check that with the team for you.

turns.line: Okay. There’s a lot to take in.
turns.goal: Invite a question and check understanding in a supportive way.
turns.example: Of course. What would you like me to go over again? Could you tell me in your own words what we agreed?
turns.phrase: What would you like me to go over again?

title: Give a clear handover
description: Organise a concise update and ask for confirmation.
facts: Taylor has asked when the team will visit.
No visit time has been confirmed. Do not add clinical findings.

turns.line: I’m taking over. Could you give me a quick update?
turns.goal: Identify the patient and state the known situation.
turns.example: This is about Taylor in room 4. Taylor has asked when the team will visit.
turns.phrase: This is about Taylor in room 4.

turns.line: Has a visit time been confirmed?
turns.example: No visit time has been confirmed. I haven’t given Taylor a time.
turns.phrase: That has not been confirmed yet.

turns.goal: State the request and close the loop.
turns.example: Could you check the visit time with the team and update Taylor? Can I confirm you’ll follow that up?
turns.phrase: Can I confirm who will follow that up?

title: Ask for clarification
description: Speak up when a message is unclear or incomplete.
facts: A colleague asks you to prepare a room.
The room number and timing are missing.
Confirm the details rather than making assumptions.

turns.line: Could you get the room ready, please?
turns.goal: Ask for the missing room number politely.
turns.example: Of course. Could you clarify which room you mean?
turns.phrase: Could you clarify which room you mean?

turns.example: Thank you. When does room six need to be ready?
turns.phrase: When does it need to be ready?

turns.line: Before the team arrives at two.
turns.example: Just to confirm: room six, ready before two. Is that correct?
turns.phrase: Just to confirm, have I understood that correctly?

title: Respond to a worried relative
description: Show empathy while respecting privacy and uncertainty.
facts: Robin asks about a fictional patient.
You have no confirmed update to share.
Check identity and consent through the appropriate local process.

turns.line: Nobody is telling me anything. What is going on?
turns.goal: Acknowledge the concern without becoming defensive.
turns.example: I can hear how worrying this is. Thank you for telling me.
turns.phrase: I can hear how worrying this is for you.

turns.line: Can you just tell me the results?
turns.goal: Explain that privacy and consent must be checked.
turns.example: Before sharing any information, I need to check identity and consent with the team.
turns.phrase: I need to check consent before sharing information.

turns.goal: Offer a clear next communication step.
turns.example: I can ask the team who can provide an update. What is the best way for them to contact you?
turns.phrase: I can ask the team who can provide an update.

title: Make an explanation clearer
description: Use plain language and a friendly understanding check.
facts: Casey received a leaflet about an appointment.
The appointment time is 10 am at reception.
No treatment instructions are part of this exercise.

turns.line: I don’t understand this appointment letter.
turns.goal: Invite the patient to identify what is confusing.
turns.example: Of course. Which part would you like us to go through together?
turns.phrase: Which part would you like us to go through together?

turns.line: Where do I go, and when?
turns.goal: Share the two supplied facts simply.
turns.example: Please come to reception at 10 am for your appointment.
turns.phrase: Please come to reception at 10 am.

turns.line: I think I’ve got it now.
turns.goal: Check understanding without testing or blaming.
turns.example: Just so I know I explained it clearly, could you tell me where you’ll go and at what time?
turns.phrase: Just so I know I explained it clearly, could you tell me the next step?

title: Handle a difficult request
description: Set a respectful boundary and offer a practical next step.
facts: Drew asks for an appointment time you cannot confirm.
The booking team holds the appointment schedule.
Acknowledge frustration without promising a date.

turns.line: I need you to guarantee I’ll be seen tomorrow.
turns.goal: Acknowledge the need without making a guarantee.
turns.example: I understand that the timing matters to you. I can’t confirm tomorrow’s appointment.
turns.phrase: I understand that the timing matters to you.

turns.line: Why can’t you just sort it out?
turns.goal: Explain your boundary simply and respectfully.
turns.example: The booking team manages the schedule. I don’t have a confirmed time to give you.
turns.phrase: I don’t have a confirmed time to give you.

turns.line: What am I supposed to do then?
turns.goal: Offer a useful next communication step.
turns.example: I can help you contact the booking team to ask about available appointments.
turns.phrase: I can help you contact the right team.
